analysis.one_liner: Requires power plants, incinerators, chemical and cement plants to cut their mercury emissions by 95 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House; it was referred to the Commerce Committee on May 5, 1998 and sent to a subcommittee three weeks later, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to force the EPA to set rules requiring the country's biggest mercury emitters — coal- and oil-fired power plants, large industrial boilers, solid-waste incinerators, mercury-cell chlorine plants, and Portland cement plants — to cut their annual mercury emissions by at least 95 percent. It would have required permits, monitoring, and public reporting of each facility's emissions, and set up programs to label mercury-containing products, warn people about contaminated fish, and study mercury's health effects on pregnant women and children. It never advanced past the committee stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to mercury pollution: pregnant women and their fetuses, young children, and people who eat a lot of freshwater fish, who are the groups most at risk from mercury's neurological effects. The bill's own findings note that 39 states had issued warnings about mercury-tainted fish in 1997, up from 27 in 1993, and that the number of mercury advisories grew 86 percent between 1993 and 1996.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families exposed to mercury through fish and air

how_it_helps.text: Requires each covered power plant, boiler, incinerator, chlor-alkali plant, and cement plant to reduce annual mercury emissions below its baseline by at least 95 percent, with enforceable permits issued within two years.
Requires the EPA to publish facility-specific mercury emission data for every covered plant each year, so residents can see what is being emitted near them.

Directs the EPA to run a public-awareness program for populations most at risk from mercury, evaluate state fish-consumption advisories for consistency, and report on mercury contamination in the Great Lakes, Chesapeake Bay, and other waters.

Requires manufacturers to label mercury-containing products such as batteries, fluorescent bulbs, and thermostats, and requires incinerators to pull those items out of the waste stream before burning.
Requires captured mercury to be disposed of so hazards are not simply moved from air to water or soil, and funds long-term research on safe disposal methods.

analysis.who_pays: The covered industries — electric utilities burning coal and oil, industrial boiler operators, waste incinerators, mercury-cell chlor-alkali plants, and cement plants — would bear the cost of controls, monitoring, permits, and reporting, and would likely pass some of it to electricity customers and consumers of their products.
analysis.who_pays_short: Utilities, incinerators, cement and chemical plants

drawbacks.text: A flat 95 percent reduction applied to every unit is a demanding target, especially for 1998-era control technology; the bill allows flexibility in control methods and trading only among units at a single site, which limits the cheaper compliance paths a plant-wide or national trading scheme would offer.

Compliance and monitoring costs at hundreds of power plants, boilers, and incinerators would be substantial, and a share would show up in electricity bills and product prices; the bill contains no cost estimates or phase-in beyond a two-year permit deadline.

Manufacturers of batteries, fluorescent lamps, thermostats, and other listed products would face new labeling and packaging obligations, and municipal and private incinerator operators would have to build source-separation and recycling programs within tight deadlines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes were high: mercury is a neurotoxin that concentrates in fish and reaches people through food, and the bill's findings cite EPA's own Mercury Study Report identifying power plants as the largest U.S. source. The costs were real but conventional pollution-control costs of the kind industry has absorbed under other Clean Air Act programs. The main design criticism is the rigid 95 percent floor applied to every unit with only same-site trading, which would have been more expensive than a market-wide trading program — but the bill's defenders would say that rigidity was the point, since it guaranteed actual reductions at every plant rather than allowing some plants to buy their way out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1998, referred to the House Commerce Committee, sent to its Health and Environment subcommittee three weeks later, and never moved again before the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Allen of Maine introduced the Omnibus Mercury Emissions Reduction Act of 1998 on May 5, 1998, joined by seven original cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
On May 26, 1998, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the last action of record is the subcommittee referral, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
The bill's findings rely on EPA's Mercury Study Report to Congress, which ranked fossil-fuel power plants first and solid-waste incinerators second among U.S. mercury emission sources.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries the bill targeted — coal- and oil-fired power plants, waste incinerators, mercury-cell chlor-alkali plants, and cement plants — were better off because it died, since they avoided mandatory 95 percent mercury cuts, permits, monitoring, and public reporting. Federal limits on power-plant mercury did not arrive until EPA rules years later, so emissions went unregulated at the federal level in the meantime.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-fired utilities and other covered emitters

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent (Sanders); no Republicans sponsored the bill, and no votes were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have required a 95 percent cut in mercury emissions, enforceable permits, monitoring, and annual public reporting — the EPA study the bill cites ranked utilities as the largest U.S. mercury source. Defeating it left power-plant mercury unregulated at the federal level, and utilities avoided the compliance cost.

industries.industry: Mercury-cell chlor-alkali (chlorine and caustic soda) producers
industries.note: Mercury-cell plants would have had to cut direct and fugitive mercury emissions 95 percent, pressuring the technology itself. The bill's death left their emissions outside a binding federal mercury standard.

Operators would have had to separate mercury items from incoming waste, submit compliance plans, and accept tighter permits, but the labeling and separation system could also have cut the mercury load they burn. The net effect for the industry was cost.

Kilns, clinker coolers, and dust-handling operations would have faced a 95 percent mercury reduction and permits within two years. The bill never advanced, so cement plants faced no new federal mercury mandate.
The bill would have required mercury-content labeling on listed products, with packaging labels for button-cell batteries too small to mark, raising modest compliance costs.
